# Overlapping claims resolve by registration order when the clock ticks

## Context

`test/playwright/unit/manager/DragCoordinator.spec.mjs:633` — *"THE OVERLAP FALSIFIER: three overlapping windows, one gesture → exactly ONE preview and exactly ONE commit"* — is the witness ADR 0029 §2.8.1 declares **binding** on the claim-arbitration leaf (#15246). It asserts a named winner:

```js
expect([...previewIds]).toEqual(['workspace-a']);   // "the deterministic winner"
```

It has now been observed producing **all three** candidate values:

| run | environment | received |
|---|---|---|
| local full `unit`, run 1 of 3 | macOS, `npm run test-unit` | `workspace-b` |
| local full `unit`, runs 2 and 3 · spec in isolation | same | `workspace-a` ✅ |
| CI `unit` @ `1a0dd8f108` | ubuntu runner | **`workspace-c`** ([run 33379217607](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/actions/runs/33379217607)) |

Those observations were recorded on `#17796` as a fresh instance of its "arbitrary casualty" pattern. They are **not** that pattern: this one has a single named cause, reproduced deterministically below, and it belongs to the claim protocol rather than to test infrastructure. Filed separately so `#17796` keeps owning the unexplained class.

## The Problem

`src/manager/GestureClaimArbiter.mjs:70` reads the clock **once per `claim()` call**:

```js
claim(stableId, zone) {
    const timestamp = now(),          // ← one wall-clock read per zone
          ...
          record    = {acquiredAt: live ? existing.acquiredAt : timestamp, ...};
```

`src/manager/DragCoordinator.mjs:705` raises every overlapping zone's claim inside **one synchronous pass** over the sort group:

```js
if (intersects && accepts) {
    arbiter.claim(zone.stableTargetId, zone)
} else {
    arbiter.release(zone.stableTargetId)
}
```

Each iteration does real work before its `claim()` — `Window.get(windowId)?.innerRect`, an `intersects()` test, the zone's own `acceptsRemoteDrag()` hit-test, and the candidates bookkeeping. So a millisecond boundary can fall **between** two claims of the same pass. When it does, `resolve()`'s primary axis (`record.acquiredAt < winner.acquiredAt`) separates zones that the gesture treated as simultaneous, and the lexicographic tiebreak — the axis that makes the outcome deterministic — never runs.

**What wins instead is the iteration order of the sort group, i.e. registration order** — precisely what §2.8.1 exists to replace ("never registration/insertion order").

### Reproducer

The falsifier registers `workspace-c`, `workspace-b`, `workspace-a` in that order (reverse-lexicographic, deliberately). Driving the arbiter directly with a clock that ticks once at a chosen point in the pass:

```js
import {createGestureClaimArbiter} from './src/manager/GestureClaimArbiter.mjs';

const order = ['workspace-c', 'workspace-b', 'workspace-a'];

function run(tickAfter) {
    let t = 1000, n = 0;
    const arbiter = createGestureClaimArbiter({now: () => {
        const v = t; if (++n === tickAfter) { t += 1 } return v
    }});
    for (const id of order) { arbiter.claim(id, {id}) }
    return arbiter.resolve()?.stableId
}
```

```
no ms boundary inside the pass      -> workspace-a
boundary after the 1st claim (C)    -> workspace-c
boundary after the 2nd claim (C,B)  -> workspace-b
```

**Every observed value is reproduced, and the mapping is exact:** the CI casualty (`workspace-c`) is the boundary landing after the first claim; the local casualty (`workspace-b`) is the boundary landing after the second. Nothing else is needed to explain the three-way split — no resource pressure, no worker pollution, no spec-order leak.

### Why it presents as a flake

The pass is fast, so *usually* all three claims land in one millisecond and the intended tiebreak governs. The defect only surfaces when the loop straddles a boundary — more often on a loaded CI runner than on an idle seat, and essentially never when the spec runs in isolation. That is the exact signature that gets written off as "flaky", and it taxes the merge gate every lane is read against.

## The Architectural Reality

- `src/manager/GestureClaimArbiter.mjs:22-24` — the JSDoc states the intent precisely: *"tie — earliest acquisition wins, with stable-id lexicographic order as the final tiebreak (two claims in the same clock millisecond stay deterministic)"*. The contract is right; the implementation reaches it only by luck, because nothing makes same-pass claims share a millisecond.
- `src/manager/GestureClaimArbiter.mjs:104-120` — `resolve()` compares `acquiredAt` first and `stableId` only on exact equality. Correct given its inputs; the wrong inputs are manufactured upstream.
- `src/manager/DragCoordinator.mjs:660-710` — `resolveClaimedTarget()` is the sole `claim()` call site, and it is the pass. The acquisition instant that is *true* for every zone in it is the instant of the pointer event, not of the loop iteration.
- **Seniority across passes is unaffected.** The "earliest valid claim wins" axis measures hover seniority *within the gesture* — which zone the pointer entered first across successive moves. Successive passes still carry distinct instants, so that axis keeps working; only the false intra-pass ordering is removed.
- `learn/agentos/decisions/0029-docking-design.md:351` (§2.8.1) — the governing contract, including the binding ≥3-window falsifier. The current behavior violates it under load rather than amending it.
- The arbiter's own spec (`test/playwright/unit/manager/GestureClaimArbiter.spec.mjs`) injects a hand-advanced clock, so no existing witness exercises a real-clock pass. That is why this reached the coordinator tier unguarded.

## The Fix

Sample the clock **once per claim pass** and let every claim of that pass share the instant.

- `GestureClaimArbiter.claim(stableId, zone, timestamp = now())` — accept the pass instant; default preserves today's behavior for single-claim callers and keeps the factory pure and clock-injectable.
- `DragCoordinator.resolveClaimedTarget()` — read the clock once before the loop and thread it through every `claim()` of that pass.
- Update the arbiter JSDoc so the same-millisecond guarantee is stated as a property of the pass, not an accident of speed.

**Rejected alternative — quantize inside the arbiter** (cache a timestamp and invalidate it on a microtask): hides the pass boundary in implicit state, makes the pure factory time-order-dependent, and is untestable with an injected clock. The pass is the caller's concept; the caller should name it.

**Rejected alternative — relax the assertion** (accept any of the three winners): destroys the binding falsifier of §2.8.1 and converts a real non-determinism into documentation. Explicitly out of scope.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Every claim raised within one `resolveClaimedTarget()` pass shares one acquisition instant, so `resolve()` reaches the lexicographic tiebreak for zones the gesture treats as simultaneous.
- [ ] A `GestureClaimArbiter` witness with an injected clock that **ticks between claims of one pass** resolves to the lexicographic winner. It must fail against the current implementation — the mutation control is the tick position, and the two positions reproducing `workspace-c` and `workspace-b` are both covered.
- [ ] `THE OVERLAP FALSIFIER` at `DragCoordinator.spec.mjs:633` no longer depends on the pass fitting inside one millisecond; a witness pins the coordinator tier with a clock that ticks mid-pass.
- [ ] Hover seniority across successive moves is unchanged and still witnessed: a zone claimed on an earlier move still outranks one first claimed on a later move.
- [ ] `npm run test-unit` green, and the `unit` job green on CI (the plane where `workspace-c` was observed).

## Out of Scope

- The unexplained arbitrary-casualty class — `#17796` owns it. This ticket removes one instance from that population; it does not close it.
- The pinned legacy registration-order path for zones without a stable identity (`DragCoordinator.mjs:775-795`). That nondeterminism is deliberate, witnessed, and unchanged here.
- Any change to §2.8.1's semantics. This restores the documented behavior; it does not amend the ADR.
- The claim TTL / expiry axis, which is independently witnessed with an injected clock.

## Avoided Traps

- **Reading the green as the truth.** The assertion passes on most runs, which is exactly why the defect survived: an outcome that is *usually* deterministic reads as deterministic.
- **Blaming the harness.** The three-value split has an infrastructure *signature* (load-selected, isolation-clean) but a product cause; attributing it to worker pollution would have left the arbiter unfixed.
- **Trusting the JSDoc as the guarantee.** The file states the same-millisecond property plainly; nothing enforced it. A doc claiming a guard is not a guard.
- **Fixing it in the spec.** A 1ms clock spin was used during #15246 to disambiguate the arbiter spec's *seniority* witness — legitimate there, since that witness is about age. Spinning the clock to stabilize a *tie* witness would hide this defect instead of surfacing it.

## Decision Record impact

`aligned-with ADR 0029` (§2.8.1). The change makes the implementation obey the stated tie contract; it does not modify, amend, or challenge it.

## Contract Ledger

The formal contract surface for the arbiter/coordinator changes shipped by PR #17936. Backfilled here on the ticket body per RA-1 (@neo-gpt, round 1). Two comments hold the drafting history — the [original rows](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/17934#issuecomment-5477146711) and [my correction of them](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/17934#issuecomment-5477234664) — but this table is the authoritative one, and it supersedes both.

| Target Surface | Source of Authority | Behavior | Fallback | Docs | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `arbiter.passInstant()` | §2.8.1 claim protocol (ADR 0029) — the winner must not depend on caller iteration order | Samples **one** acquisition instant per claim pass, from the **arbiter's own** clock. A caller evaluating several zones against a single pointer event calls this once and passes the result to every `claim()` of that pass | None by construction — a caller that never calls it gets `claim()`'s per-call default, identical for a single-claim pass | JSDoc on `passInstant()`, plus the "One instant per claim pass" block in the class doc | `GestureClaimArbiter.spec.mjs` ticking-clock arms: a clock advancing between calls within one pass no longer changes the winner |
| `arbiter.claim(stableId, zone, timestamp = now())` | §2.8.1 tie rule, and the TTL property "a claim lives `claimTtlMs` after its last refresh" | **Two deliberately separate axes.** `acquiredAt` takes the **pass instant** — seniority, shared across the pass, so same-pass claims tie and resolve lexicographically rather than by acquisition order. `live` and `expiresAt` take **`now()` at refresh** — lifetime is a wall-clock fact | **Backward-compatible default:** omitting `timestamp` reads the clock per call, exactly what every existing single-claim caller already did — for a one-claim pass the two reads are the same value | JSDoc on `claim()`, naming both axes and why the default exists | Slow-pass arm (a claim raised 150ms into a 100ms TTL is live for a full TTL from its own refresh) and mid-pass-expiry arm (a record that lapsed mid-pass reacquires rather than reviving) |
| `DragCoordinator.resolveClaimedTarget()` | §2.8.1, and the defect this ticket closes | Consumes **one** instant per pass: samples `passInstant()` once, then hands it to every `claim()` raised for that pointer event | If the arbiter is absent the coordinator's prior path is unchanged — the instant is threaded only where a claim is actually raised | JSDoc at the call site | `DragCoordinator.spec.mjs` — the OVERLAP FALSIFIER holds its stated "deterministic winner" under a clock that ticks mid-pass |

### Non-regression these rows must not be read as weakening

**Cross-pass seniority is untouched.** Sharing an instant applies *within* one pass only; successive passes carry successive instants, so a genuinely earlier claim still outranks a later one. What the change removes is a *false* seniority — between zones that became hoverable simultaneously and therefore carry no ordering relative to each other.

**TTL is measured from the last refresh, and that is a change.** An earlier draft of this ledger claimed TTL behaviour was unchanged. It was wrong, and the refutation sat inside its own sentence ("rather than instants a millisecond apart" assumes a pass takes a millisecond — the whole defect is what happens when it does not). The shipped code reads liveness and expiry from `now()` at refresh, never from the pass instant; deriving `expiresAt` from a pass *start* makes a claim raised late in a slow pass arrive already expired, inverting the property the TTL exists to state.

### Why a tie is the correct resolution rather than a finer clock

Zones evaluated against a single pointer event became hoverable at the same moment. Any ordering between them is an artifact of the caller's iteration, not a fact about the gesture — so the honest model is a **tie**, resolved by the lexicographic tiebreak §2.8.1 already defines. Reading the clock per call does not produce a better ordering; it produces a *millisecond-boundary-dependent* one, where whether two claims tie depends on whether the pass straddled a tick. That is precisely the observed nondeterminism.

### Evidence standard, stated honestly

Each expiry arm is pinned by mutation: reverting the liveness read to the pass instant must red it. That held for the slow-pass arm from the start. It did **not** hold for the mid-pass-expiry arm as first shipped — @neo-gpt caught this in round 2 (RA-2), and he was right. That arm gave its existing record and its pass instant the same value (`1_000`), so `existing.acquiredAt` and the supplied `timestamp` coincided and the assertion read identically on both sides of the boundary it claimed to pin. It is repaired at `c86e777fe6` by separating the three instants — acquisition `900`, pass `950`, refresh `1_100` — so the shipped path carries `acquiredAt=950` while the mutation carries `900`. Verified both ways: 20/20 green as shipped; the mutation fails on that exact line (`Expected: 950, Received: 900`) with the other 19 arms untouched, so the red is the named defect and not collateral.

## Correction to my own ledger: the TTL row was wrong

@neo-gpt's RA-2 refutes a claim I made in [the ledger comment above](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/17934#issuecomment-5477146711). I wrote:

> TTL behaviour is unchanged: it is measured from the recorded instant, and within a pass every claim now records the same one rather than instants a millisecond apart.

**That is false, and the refutation was sitting inside the sentence.** "Rather than instants a millisecond apart" assumes a pass takes a millisecond. The entire defect is what happens when it does not.

### The defect, reproduced

`GestureClaimArbiter.claim()` used the pass instant for **both** axes:

```js
live      = existing != null && existing.expiresAt >= timestamp,   // ← pass instant
expiresAt : timestamp + claimTtlMs,                                 // ← pass instant
```

With `claimTtlMs: 100`, a claim raised 150ms after `passInstant()` was created with `expiresAt` already behind the current clock — **born expired, immediately unresolvable**, despite having just been refreshed. That inverts the one property the TTL states: a claim lives `claimTtlMs` after its **last refresh**. The same stale read also pinned an existing record *alive* across an expiry it had genuinely passed.

### The fix, at `a4b1b423e8`

Split the axes. The pass instant is seniority and nothing else; liveness and expiry read the real clock at refresh:

```js
refreshedAt = now(),
live        = existing != null && existing.expiresAt >= refreshedAt,
acquiredAt  : live ? existing.acquiredAt : timestamp,   // seniority — the pass instant
expiresAt   : refreshedAt + claimTtlMs,                 // lifetime — this refresh
```

Cross-pass seniority is genuinely untouched — that part of my ledger row stands. Two witnesses at the boundary: a claim raised 150ms into a 100ms-TTL pass resolves and stays resolvable for a full TTL from its own refresh; a record that expired mid-pass reacquires rather than reviving. Reverting either read reds exactly those two arms and nothing else.

### The corrected ledger row

| Target Surface | Proposed Behavior | Fallback | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `arbiter.claim(stableId, zone, timestamp = now())` | `acquiredAt` takes the **pass instant** (seniority, shared across the pass). `live` and `expiresAt` take **`now()` at refresh** (lifetime). The two axes are deliberately separate | Default `timestamp = now()` keeps single-claim callers unchanged | Slow-pass and mid-pass-expiry arms in `GestureClaimArbiter.spec.mjs`; both red against the pass-instant expiry |

### One more thing the fix disturbed, and why it is not a recalibration

The negative witness pinned `runPass(2, false) === 'workspace-b'`. Adding the separate refresh read changes how many times `claim()` reads the clock, so the ticking-clock boundary lands elsewhere and that arm reddened — **without its subject having changed at all**.

I did not renumber it to green. The arm now asserts the property: sweeping every boundary, an unshared pass yields more than one distinct winner (the defect), while a shared pass yields `workspace-a` everywhere (the fix). That is read-count independent and strictly stronger than the three hand-picked cases. **A test pinned to a boundary→winner table was encoding an implementation detail as a contract**, which is the same class of mistake as the ledger row above: stating an incidental as an invariant.

reads the clock — adding the refresh read moved the boundary and reddened an arm
whose subject had not changed. It now sweeps every boundary and asserts the
defect itself: unshared, the winner is a function of where the millisecond fell;
shared, it is lexicographic everywhere. Strictly stronger than the three
hand-picked cases it replaces.

* test(manager): make the mid-pass expiry arm kill its mutation (#17934)

The existing-record arm asserted a boundary it could not witness. Its
acquisition instant and its pass instant were the same number (1_000), so
`existing.acquiredAt` and the freshly supplied `timestamp` coincided:
reverting the liveness read from `refreshedAt` back to `timestamp` produced
an identical `acquiredAt=1_000`, `expiresAt=1_300` and winning zone. The arm
passed on both sides of the boundary it was written to pin.

Separating the three instants — acquisition 900, pass 950, refresh 1_100 —
makes the shipped reacquisition carry 950 while the stale-pass-liveness
mutation carries 900. Verified both ways: 20/20 green as shipped, and the
mutation fails on exactly that line (Expected 950, Received 900) with the
other 19 arms untouched, so the red is the named defect and not collateral.
